title: Interest Rates, the Yield Curve and Central Banks
intro: Interest rates are the price of money over time, and they move every asset: higher rates lower the present value of future cash, make borrowing dearer and pull money into bonds and deposits. This page explains how central banks set short rates, how markets set long ones, and what the shape of the yield curve says.

blocks.text: Central banks and the policy rate

A central bank sets the shortest interest rates in its currency and acts as lender of last resort to banks. The main ones are the US Federal Reserve (the Fed), the European Central Bank (ECB), the Bank of Japan (BoJ), the Bank of England (BoE), the Swiss National Bank (SNB) and the People's Bank of China (PBoC). Most have a mandate of stable prices, usually defined as about 2% inflation, and the Fed also has maximum employment (the 'dual mandate').

items: The Fed's main tool is the target range for the federal funds rate, the rate at which banks lend each other reserves overnight, set eight times a year by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). It steers it by paying interest on reserves and through repo operations; the secured overnight rate SOFR has replaced LIBOR as the benchmark for loans and derivatives.
The ECB sets a deposit facility rate; the Bank of England sets Bank Rate; the BoJ has its own short-term policy rate, which it held below zero from 2016 to 2024.

Quantitative easing (QE): buying long-term government bonds and MBS with newly created reserves, to push long yields down when short rates are already near zero. Quantitative tightening (QT) runs the balance sheet down again.
Forward guidance: telling markets where rates are likely to go, which moves longer yields today.

blocks.text: Raising rates slows the economy (borrowing costs more, saving pays more, asset prices and the currency react) and with a lag of a year or more brings inflation down. Cutting rates does the opposite. The Taylor rule (John Taylor, 1993) is a widely used benchmark for where the policy rate 'should' be:

blocks.text: From short rates to long rates

Long yields are set by the market. Under the expectations hypothesis, a long yield is the average of expected future short rates; in practice investors also want a term premium for locking money up and bearing duration risk:

Because markets look ahead, long yields often move before the central bank does, and a rate cut that was expected moves nothing on the day. Long yields also respond to inflation expectations, government borrowing, foreign demand for the currency and the supply of bonds.

Today's yields imply forward rates, the rates you can lock in now for future borrowing. With a one-year yield $y_1$ and a two-year yield $y_2$ (both yearly), the one-year rate one year from now, $f_{1,1}$, satisfies

If $y_1 = 4\%$ and $y_2 = 4.5\%$, then $f_{1,1} = 1.045^2/1.04 - 1 \approx 5.0\%$. Forward rates are the market's break-even: if next year's one-year rate comes in below 5%, the two-year bond was the better buy.
The yield curve plots government yields against maturity. Its shape is one of the most-watched signals in finance:

blocks.alt: Three yield curve shapes plotted as yield against maturity from 3 months to 30 years: a normal upward-sloping curve, a flat curve, and an inverted curve where short-term yields are higher than long-term yields.
blocks.caption: Normal, flat and inverted yield curves (illustrative).

items: Normal (upward sloping): long yields above short ones; the usual state, from expected rate rises and the term premium.
Flat: the market expects rates to stay about where they are, often late in a tightening cycle.

Inverted: short yields above long ones; the market expects cuts, usually because it expects the economy to weaken. The 10-year minus 3-month spread inverted before every US recession since the late 1960s, with lead times of roughly 6 to 24 months; it also inverted in 2022-23 with no US recession declared in the two years that followed, so it is a signal, not a law.
Steepening and flattening: changes in the slope. A 'bull steepener' (short yields falling faster) often happens when the central bank starts cutting.

blocks.text: Real rates, inflation and asset prices

The real interest rate (nominal yield minus expected inflation, or directly the TIPS yield) is what matters for valuations. When the 10-year real yield rose from about −1% to about +1.5% during 2022 (and 2% in 2023), long bonds and growth stocks, whose value lies far in the future, fell sharply, and gold, which pays nothing, dropped about 20% from its March peak. Lower real rates push the other way. The same present-value arithmetic links all of them.
Inflation and how it is measured

items: CPI (consumer price index) measures a basket of consumer prices; core CPI excludes food and energy, which are volatile.
The Fed targets the PCE price index, which covers a broader set of spending and adjusts the basket faster.
Inflation is driven by demand outrunning supply, by supply shocks (oil in 1973 and 1979, pandemic bottlenecks and energy in 2021-22), by wages and expectations, and over the long run by money growth.

blocks.text: The 1-year yield is 3.5% and the 2-year yield is 4.0% (yearly compounding). What 1-year rate one year ahead does this imply?

blocks.title: Taylor rule
blocks.text: The neutral real rate is 0.5%, inflation is 4% against a 2% target, and the output gap is +1%. What policy rate does the Taylor rule suggest?

blocks.title: Reading the curve
blocks.text: Three-month bills yield 5.3%, 2-year notes 4.7% and 10-year notes 4.1%. What shape is the curve, and what is the market probably expecting?
solution: It is inverted: yields fall with maturity. The market expects the central bank to cut rates over the next few years, usually because it expects slower growth or lower inflation. Historically such inversions have often preceded recessions, though not always.
